screens.title: Touching ends
screens.prose: Closed $[1, 4]$ and $[4, 5]$ share the point 4. Meetings are booked half-open: $[0, 10)$ ends just before 10, so the room is free at 10. This is the convention from `contests` l10-greedy-proofs.
screens.question: Which pairs overlap?

options.text: Both pairs: the closed pair and the meetings
options.why: You read the meetings as closed. A meeting that ends at 10 has left the room at 10.

options.text: Neither pair: touching ends never overlap
options.why: Closed $[1, 4]$ holds 4, and so does $[4, 5]$. They share a point, so they merge.

options.text: Only the two meetings, not the closed pair
options.why: You swapped the conventions. Half-open intervals that touch do not overlap; closed ones do.

hints.text: Which pair is closed at the shared point?
$[0, 10)$ does not contain 10.
The closed pair shares 4 and merges to $[1, 5]$. The meetings share nothing, so both fit in one room.

feedback.correct: Closed ends that touch merge. Half-open ends that touch do not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask, for each pair, whether the shared point belongs to both.

byKey.b: You treated $[0, 10)$ as if it held 10. The round bracket says it does not.
byKey.c: You treated $[1, 4]$ as if it stopped before 4. The square bracket says 4 is in.

explain.text: For closed intervals the merge test is `s <= last_end`, so equal points join. For half-open ones it is `s < last_end`, so touching ends stay apart. Read the brackets before you write the comparison.

screens.title: Write the merge
screens.prose: Intervals `[start, end]` hold whole numbers, come in any order, and may overlap or touch. Return the merged list, sorted by start, as lists. Two intervals that share an end point merge.
screens.question: Write `merge_intervals(intervals)`.

widget.how: Check runs 11 hidden tests: touching ends, an empty list, one interval and unsorted input. Others hold a long first interval, negatives, repeats and a merge into a later block. Each result must equal the expected list.

hints.text: After sorting, which interval can the next one merge with?
Only the last interval in `out` can overlap the next one.
Loop over `sorted(intervals)`. If `out` is not empty and `s <= out[-1][1]`, set `out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)`; otherwise append `[s, e]`.

feedback.correct: One sort, then one pass: $O(n \log n)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 needs $[2, 5]$ and $[4, 9]$ joined into $[2, 9]$. Sorting alone leaves them apart.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 touches at 4. Use `<=`, so a shared end point merges.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 has $[2, 3]$ inside $[1, 10]$. Keep the larger end with `max`.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check the empty list: `out[-1]` fails until `out` holds something.

explain.text: After the sort, a new interval can only overlap the last merged one. `max` keeps a long interval's end when a short one falls inside it. The sort costs $O(n \log n)$ and the pass $O(n)$.

screens.title: The pattern
screens.prose:
What you wrote, as a pattern:

```python
out = []
for s, e in sorted(intervals):    # by start
    if out and s <= out[-1][1]:    # overlap
        out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)
    else:
        out.append([s, e])          # new block
```
screens.question: Put the steps of the merge in order. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: Start the output with the first interval
Compare the next start with the last merged end
If the start is at most that end, extend the end with max; else append
Compare the end of the new interval with the last end
lines.why: The ends do not decide an overlap. After the sort, a new interval overlaps when its start is at most the last end.

feedback.correct: Sort, seed, compare, extend or append, return.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The sort has to come before any comparison.

byKey.d1: You compared the two ends. An interval with a larger end can still start after the block ends.
byKey.left-out: Every step but one belongs. Only the step about comparing ends is wrong.

explain.text: The sort makes the last block the only one a new interval can touch. The start-against-end test decides overlap, and `max` decides the new end. Each interval is looked at once after the sort.

screens.title: Overlapping orders
screens.prose: Each resting order in a book lives for a half-open span `[start, end)` in milliseconds. Two orders overlap if both rest at some moment. In `contests` l10 a sweep counted rooms. Here, at each start, add how many orders are already active.
screens.question: Write `count_overlapping_pairs(intervals)` for half-open intervals with `start < end`. Touching ends do not overlap.

tests.setup: iv = [[i, i + 3] for i in range(100000)]

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests: touching ends, no orders, three equal orders, and a long order over short ones. Test 8 has 100,000 orders, so a double loop over pairs cannot finish in time.

hints.text: Turn each order into two events: it starts, and it ends.
At equal times an end must come before a start.
Build `(s, 1)` and `(e, -1)` and sort them. At a start add `active` to `pairs`, then add the step to `active`.

feedback.correct: Each start meets every order still active: one sort, one pass.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 touches at 10. Sort the end, `(10, -1)`, before the start, `(10, 1)`; tuples do that for you.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 has three equal orders: pairs 0 + 1 + 2 = 3. Count before you add the start to `active`.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 timed out. A double loop makes about 5 billion checks; the sweep makes 200,000 events.

explain.text: A pair overlaps exactly when the later start finds the earlier order still active. So the sum of `active` at every start counts each pair once. Sorting `(time, -1)` before `(time, 1)` keeps touching orders apart.

quiz.prose: A merge sorts one million intervals first. Sorting makes about $n \log_2 n$ comparisons.
quiz.question: About how many comparisons is that?

options.why: You counted one look per interval. A sort makes about $\log_2 n \approx 20$ comparisons per item.
You used $\log_{10}$. A comparison sort halves the problem, so the log is base 2.
That is $n^2$, the cost of comparing every pair. A good sort is far cheaper.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply $n$ by $\log_2 n$.

explain.text: $\log_2 10^6 = 6 \log_2 10 \approx 19.93$. So the sort makes about 19.9 million comparisons, and the merge pass adds one million more.

quiz.prose: To count overlapping pairs among $n = 100{,}000$ orders, a double loop checks every pair once. The sweep instead sorts and walks $2n$ events.
quiz.question: How many pair checks does the double loop make?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count each unordered pair once.

byKey.ordered: That is $n^2$. It counts each pair twice and pairs each order with itself.
byKey.ordered2: That is $n(n - 1)$, each pair in both orders. Halve it.
byKey.events: That is the sweep's event count. The question asks about the double loop.

explain.text: The double loop checks $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ pairs, about 5 billion here. The sweep sorts $2n = 200{,}000$ events and walks them once. That is why test 8 needs the sweep.
